predictions.explanation:
Key facts:

- **January 6 prosecutions.** The Justice Department’s Jan. 6 investigation is the largest in U.S. history. By around the fourth anniversary, roughly **1,500–1,575 individuals** had been federally charged in connection with the Capitol attack, and over 1,000 had been convicted or pleaded guilty.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cases_of_the_January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack?utm_source=openai))  Virtually all Jan. 6 cases are federal, so this is also a good approximation of the total number of prosecuted individuals.

- **2020 BLM‑era riot/looting prosecutions – federal.** A Justice Department press release (updated through Feb. 2025) states that **“more than 300 individuals”** in 29 states and D.C. have faced **federal charges for crimes committed “adjacent to or under the guise of peaceful demonstrations”** since late May 2020.([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/over-300-people-facing-federal-charges-crimes-committed-during-nationwide-demonstrations?utm_source=openai))  An Associated Press review found about **300+ federal George‑Floyd‑era protest cases**, with roughly **120 defendants convicted or pleading guilty** to federal crimes such as conspiracy, arson, or rioting.([justthenews.com](https://justthenews.com/government/courts-law/tarrio-j6-defendants-receive-long-prison-sentences-while-blm-rioters-received?utm_source=openai))  On the purely federal level, Jan. 6 clearly produced far more prosecuted individuals than the 2020 protest unrest.

- **2020 BLM‑era riot/looting prosecutions – state/local.** There is **no authoritative nationwide count** of how many distinct individuals were prosecuted for rioting or looting arising from the 2020 protests:
  * Major Cities Chiefs Association data show **16,241 protest‑related arrests** in 68 major jurisdictions between May 25 and July 31, 2020, with about **2,735 (17%)** classified as felony arrests.([govtech.com](https://www.govtech.com/em/emergency-blogs/disaster-zone/a-protest-after-action-report-from-major-city-police-chiefs-association.html?utm_source=openai))  But this is arrests, not prosecutions or convictions.
  * A Guardian analysis of a dozen cities found that **at least 90% of protest citations/charges were dropped, dismissed, or never filed** in most jurisdictions, including in cities that saw significant unrest.([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/apr/17/george-floyd-protesters-charges-citations-analysis?utm_source=openai))  That strongly implies the eventual number of prosecuted individuals was much smaller than total arrests.
  * City‑level data illustrate the scale but don’t sum to a national total: e.g., about **157 people charged** in connection with George Floyd–related unrest in Chicago, and **91 felony burglary (looting) cases** in Minneapolis–St Paul, plus a small number of other serious charges.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests_in_Chicago?utm_source=openai))  Similar pockets of prosecutions existed elsewhere, but comprehensive nationwide aggregation is lacking.

- **What we can and cannot definitively say.**
  * On **federal prosecutions alone**, Sacks’ claim is clearly borne out: **Jan. 6 produced many times more federal defendants (~1,500+) than the 2020 protests did (just 300‑plus).**([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cases_of_the_January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack?utm_source=openai))
  * However, his statement was not explicitly limited to federal court. Once you include **state and local** prosecutions for 2020 riot/looting offenses, the total number of BLM‑era defendants could plausibly approach or even exceed the Jan. 6 total—but we lack a reliable nationwide figure. We only know that most low‑level cases were dropped and that serious riot/looting cases numbered in the hundreds in some major metros, not whether the ultimate national aggregate was above or below ~1,500 individuals.

Because there is **no comprehensive, authoritative national count** of individuals prosecuted for 2020 riot/looting offenses (as opposed to arrests, or all protest‑related charges), we cannot rigorously compare that total to the well‑documented Jan. 6 prosecution count. On the evidence available, Sacks’ prediction is very likely correct for **federal** prosecutions, but **whether it is correct for *all* prosecutions (federal + state + local) cannot be determined with confidence.**

Hence the prediction is best coded as **"ambiguous"**: enough time has passed to know what prosecutions occurred, but the necessary nationwide comparative data for 2020 riot/looting cases are not available in a form that allows a definitive yes/no judgment.

predictions.grok_explanation: David Sacks predicted more prosecutions (arrests/charges based on video/evidence) for those who stormed the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol than for rioting/looting from 2020 BLM protests. As of 2025, ~1,570-1,583 individuals were federally charged for Jan. 6 involvement, identified largely via video footage and public tips ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_proceedings_in_the_January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack), [ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/US/jan-6-capitol-attack-investigation-stands-numbers-doj/story?id=117353000), [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5y7l47xrpko)). For BLM protests: total arrests ~13,600-16,000 (including non-violent like curfew violations), with ~2,735 felony arrests in major cities and ~300-350 federal charges nationwide for serious crimes like rioting/arson/looting; >120 federal guilty pleas/convictions, but many local charges dropped ([Prosecution Project](https://theprosecutionproject.org/summer-2020-protests/), [DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/over-300-people-facing-federal-charges-crimes-committed-during-nationwide-demonstrations), [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/records-rebut-claims-jan-6-rioters-55adf4d46aff57b91af2fdd3345dace8), [MCCA Report](https://majorcitieschiefs.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/MCCA-Report-on-the-2020-Protest-and-Civil-Unrest.pdf)). Even maximizing BLM serious riot/loot prosecutions, they fall short of Jan. 6 totals, confirming the prediction.

predictions.explanation: In January 2021, David Sacks argued that Donald Trump had effectively disqualified himself from ever again being a national-level candidate, implying he would not be a serious contender for the presidency in 2024 or later. In fact, Trump officially launched a 2024 presidential campaign on November 15, 2022, and went on to secure the Republican Party nomination on March 12, 2024, running as the party’s standard-bearer. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_2024_presidential_campaign?utm_source=openai)) In the general election on November 5, 2024, Trump won the presidency, receiving 312 electoral votes and roughly 49.8–49.9% of the popular vote, defeating Democratic nominee Kamala Harris. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai)) Because Trump did in fact run as a serious national candidate and was elected president again, the prediction that his national-level candidacy was “off the table” was wrong.

predictions.explanation:
Chamath’s claim was that, after January 6, **the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY) and “every single state that can go after this guy” would go after Trump with the gloves off** in the coming years.([podscripts.co](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/all-in-with-chamath-jason-sacks-friedberg/e16-reflecting-on-the-riots-at-the-us-capitol-plus-georgia-runoff-elections-vaccine-distribution-more?utm_source=openai))

What actually happened:

* **SDNY did *not* go “gloves off” against Trump.** SDNY had been investigating the Michael Cohen hush‑money payments but, months after January 6, it *concluded that investigation and decided not to bring charges against Trump at all*.([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-118hhrg56097/html/CHRG-118hhrg56097.htm?utm_source=openai)) SDNY has not indicted Trump in any other matter since then.
* **Only a very small number of state jurisdictions actually indicted Trump.** In 2023 he was indicted on state charges only in New York (Manhattan DA’s case over falsifying business records, which led to a 2024 felony conviction) and in Georgia (Fulton County’s racketeering case over the 2020 election).([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_in_New_York?utm_source=openai)) The Georgia case was later taken over by a new prosecutor and fully dismissed in November 2025, ending that state’s criminal effort.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_election_racketeering_prosecution?utm_source=openai))
* **New York state authorities were aggressive, but they were the exception, not “every single state.”** Beyond the Manhattan DA’s criminal case, New York Attorney General Letitia James pursued a sweeping civil fraud suit that resulted in a large judgment and business restrictions against Trump and his companies (later modified on appeal).([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_business_fraud_lawsuit_against_the_Trump_Organization?utm_source=openai)) Other states largely focused on Trump allies (e.g., fake‑elector prosecutions) rather than on Trump personally, and no broad wave of state criminal cases against Trump materialized.

Because SDNY *declined* to charge Trump and only a couple of state jurisdictions brought major cases (with one of those ultimately dropped), the prediction that SDNY and **“every single state that can go after this guy” would pursue him aggressively and without restraint** did **not** come true.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence shows Josh Hawley and Ted Cruz faced short‑term backlash after their January 6, 2021 objections, but their medium‑term and current political standing—especially with Republican voters and in their 2024 races—was not *ultimately* harmed and in some ways was reinforced.

1. **Immediate backlash and elite costs (real but temporary)**
   * Hawley’s high‑profile role in objecting to certification led to calls for resignation and a majority of Missouri voters saying shortly after Jan. 6 that he should resign; even about one in five Missouri Republicans agreed. His approval was underwater in that moment. ([thedailybeast.com](https://www.thedailybeast.com/show-me-state-tells-josh-hawley-to-show-himself-out-poll-finds/?utm_source=openai))
   * Simon & Schuster canceled Hawley’s book deal specifically over his role in challenging the election; the book was quickly picked up by Regnery, mitigating the damage. ([townhall.com](https://townhall.com/tipsheet/leahbarkoukis/2021/01/27/hawley-answers-whether-hes-planning-a-2024-presidential-run-n2583777?utm_source=openai))
   * Numerous major corporations publicly paused or suspended PAC donations to lawmakers who voted against certification, explicitly including Hawley and Cruz (e.g., Amazon, Microsoft, AT&T, Walmart, Marriott, Nike, etc.). ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/01/11/facebook-halts-political-donations-after-capitol-riot.html?utm_source=openai))
   * However, watchdog reports later documented that many corporations or associated PACs resumed giving—directly or via party committees—to members of the so‑called “Sedition Caucus,” blunting the long‑term financial impact. ([citizensforethics.org](https://www.citizensforethics.org/reports-investigations/crew-reports/the-corporate-insurrection-how-companies-have-broken-promises-and-funded-seditionists/?utm_source=openai))

2. **Support among Republican voters rebounded and is now very strong**
   * While Morning Consult data showed immediate post‑riot approval drops among Republicans in Missouri and Texas, majorities of GOP voters in both states still approved of Hawley and Cruz even in January 2021. ([newsweek.com](https://www.newsweek.com/josh-hawley-ted-cruz-see-approval-ratings-drop-missouri-texas-after-election-objection-riot-1563825?utm_source=openai))
   * By 2024–25, Hawley’s position with Missouri Republicans is extremely strong: SLU/YouGov polling finds about 86–88% of Missouri Republicans approving of his job performance, with roughly half “strongly approve.” ([slu.edu](https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/data-archive/february-2024-poll/write-ups/slu-yougov-poll-shows-how-missourians-rate-politicians.php?utm_source=openai))
   * Similarly, UT/Texas Politics Project polling shows Cruz with very high job‑approval and favorability among Texas Republicans (e.g., around the high‑70s to 80%+ approval in 2022–24, 73% favorable vs 12% unfavorable among Republicans in early 2024). ([texaspolitics.utexas.edu](https://texaspolitics.utexas.edu/blog/new-uttexas-politics-project-poll-primary-voting-begins-texans-see-crisis-border?utm_source=openai))
   * Broader polling indicates that Republican voters overall tended to approve of efforts to object to the 2020 results; in Georgia, for example, Republicans approved of lawmakers voting to overturn the election by a net +44 points. ([dataforprogress.org](https://www.dataforprogress.org/memos/2022/1/6/voters-disapprove-of-efforts-to-overturn-election-results?utm_source=openai))  This undercuts the specific claim that the objection would hurt Hawley and Cruz “including with Republican voters.”

3. **Electoral outcomes: both were comfortably re‑elected in 2024**
   * In November 2024, Hawley won re‑election in Missouri with 55.6% of the vote to Democrat Lucas Kunce’s 41.8%, a solid double‑digit margin in a statewide race. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Missouri?utm_source=openai))
   * Ted Cruz won re‑election to a third Senate term in Texas with 53.1% to Colin Allred’s 44.6%, improving substantially on his close 2018 margin. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Texas?utm_source=openai))  His performance exceeded late polling expectations, suggesting no decisive electoral penalty.
   * Pre‑election polling in both states consistently showed them ahead; Cook and other handicappers continued to rate Hawley’s seat as “Solid/Lean Republican,” and Texas polling showed Cruz holding clear leads and strong backing from GOP voters. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/19/congressional-fundraisers-lobby-companies-that-suspended-donations-after-capitol-riot-.html?utm_source=openai))

4. **Fundraising and intra‑GOP standing often *benefited***
   * Reporting in early 2021 found the NRSC got some of its best small‑dollar digital fundraising returns using Hawley’s name—second only to its own chair—indicating his objection enhanced his value with grassroots Republican donors rather than hurting it. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/19/congressional-fundraisers-lobby-companies-that-suspended-donations-after-capitol-riot-.html?utm_source=openai))
   * Subsequent Missouri polling shows Hawley’s overall favorability and job approval improving by 2024–25 compared with the immediate post‑riot period, with analysts noting his combative style resonates with Republican voters. ([missouriindependent.com](https://missouriindependent.com/2024/08/29/poll-shows-missouri-voters-back-trump-hawley-abortion-rights-and-minimum-wage-hike/?utm_source=openai))
   * Cruz remains one of the best‑known national GOP figures and is routinely listed among plausible 2028 presidential contenders; recent coverage of his feud with Tucker Carlson explicitly frames both as likely 2028 aspirants, not sidelined figures. ([politico.com](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/20/ted-cruz-tucker-carlson-iran-fight-00415813?utm_source=openai))

5. **2024 presidential ambitions and broader prospects**
   * Sacks tied the objection to ambitions for 2024. In reality, both men *chose not to run* for president in 2024, mainly because Donald Trump dominated the field, not because GOP voters turned against them over Jan. 6.
   * Hawley repeatedly said in January 2021 that he was not running for president and would focus on his Senate work; he later publicly ruled out a 2024 run. ([foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/josh-hawley-wont-run-for-president-in-2024?utm_source=openai))
   * Cruz openly flirted with a 2024 presidential bid but ultimately prioritized his Senate re‑election, while keeping national ambitions alive for the post‑Trump era. ([foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/2024-watch-cruz-running-senate-re-election-doesnt-rule-out-presidential-run?utm_source=openai))  His continued positioning for 2028 suggests his “future prospects” within the party remain intact.

**Bottom line:**

Their Jan. 6 objections clearly produced short‑term reputational and financial costs with national elites and general‑election audiences, but:

* They retain overwhelming support among Republican voters in their states.
* Both decisively won re‑election in 2024.
* Hawley remains a powerful figure in Missouri, and Cruz is still treated as a serious future presidential contender.

Given that their core political careers and standing with GOP voters have not been “ultimately” harmed—and in some respects were strengthened within the party—the prediction that this move would hurt rather than help their political prospects, especially among Republicans and regarding future ambitions, is best judged as **wrong** overall.

Ted Cruz won re-election in Texas, defeating Colin Allred ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_Senate_election_in_Texas), [Texas Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2024/11/05/ted-cruz-colin-allred-texas-senate-election-2024/), [Politico](https://www.politico.com/2024-election/results/texas/senate/)). Neither ran for president in 2024, but Hawley reiterated no 2024 run to focus on Senate ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/meet-the-press/meetthepressblog/hawley-reiterates-wont-run-president-rcna57235)); both remain GOP influencers (Cruz Commerce chair, 2028 speculation ([Axios](https://www.axios.com/2025/11/17/ted-cruz-tucker-carlson-president-2028))). Early Jan 6 dips in GOP approval recovered; no long-term harm evident, contrary to prediction ([Forbes Jan 2021](https://www.forbes.com/sites/alisondurkee/2021/01/22/poll-most-gop-voters-still-support-josh-hawley-ted-cruz-after-capitol-riots/), [KCUR 2022](https://www.kcur.org/news/2022-01-06/a-year-after-risking-his-career-on-jan-6-sen-josh-hawley-of-missouri-prospers-politically)). By 2025, prospects strengthened.

predictions.explanation:
Friedberg’s claim was explicitly conditional: if the U.S. adopted a highly centralized, 24/7, mass-site, nurse‑ and National Guard–driven vaccination program, he argued it *could* vaccinate essentially the whole population in 90 days. The United States did not implement anything close to that specific model. The real program combined federal coordination (Operation Warp Speed and then the Biden administration) with mostly state- and county-run clinics, hospitals, and large pharmacy chains, not a single uniform, round‑the‑clock national campaign run through mass sites and the Guard. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccination_in_the_United_States?utm_source=openai))

Empirically, the actual rollout was far slower than his 90‑day vision: the U.S. vaccination program began on December 14, 2020; by April 22, 2021 (about 130 days later), only about 27% of the total population was fully vaccinated and about 41% had received at least one dose. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/04232021.html?utm_source=openai)) By early September 2021, roughly nine months in, about 53% of the total population was fully vaccinated, and about 63% had at least one dose. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/09102021.html?utm_source=openai)) Even by mid‑July 2022, around 67% of the population was fully vaccinated and about 79% had received at least one dose—well short of “the entire country” despite far more than 90 days having elapsed. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/07152022.html?utm_source=openai))

However, because his forecast was about what *would have been possible under a different, never‑implemented system*, and not a straightforward prediction of what *did* happen under the actual U.S. strategy, the real‑world data do not directly confirm or refute his counterfactual engineering claim. The observed rollout shows that the *actual* approach did not achieve national vaccination in 90 days, but it does not definitively tell us whether his proposed centralized 90‑day plan was feasible in practice. Therefore the prediction’s accuracy is best classified as **ambiguous** rather than clearly right or wrong.

predictions.grok_explanation:
The prediction claimed that a specific centralized, 24/7, mass-site program driven by nurses and National Guard could vaccinate *essentially the entire* US population (~331 million people, requiring ~662 million doses for primary series) within 90 days. While elements like National Guard support at mass vaccination sites (e.g., NY Javits Center, federal sites with Pentagon troops) were implemented in 2021 ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/246170), [nationalguard.mil](https://www.nationalguard.mil/News/Article/2473395)), it was not a unified national program as described.

Exactly 90 days later (April 8, 2021), only 19.9% of the population (66.2 million people) were fully vaccinated ([CDC archive](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/04092021.html), [medicaleconomics.com](https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/coronavirus-vaccine-and-case-numbers-in-the-united-states-april-8-2021)). Peak daily doses reached ~4 million on April 3 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccination_in_the_United_States)), far below the ~7.3 million/day needed. Supply constraints and logistics limited feasibility early 2021. Even today (2025), primary series coverage is ~70% ([USAFacts](https://usafacts.org/visualizations/covid-vaccine-tracker-states/)), not 'entire' population.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence shows the recall organizers did obtain enough signatures to trigger a recall election, matching Chamath’s core prediction.

* **Actual deadline & signature requirement:** The California Secretary of State’s FAQ notes that, after a COVID-related court extension, the deadline to file recall petitions against Governor Gavin Newsom was **March 17, 2021**, and that the organizers needed **1,495,709 valid signatures** (12% of the votes cast in the 2018 gubernatorial election). ([sos.ca.gov](https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs?utm_source=openai))  Chamath’s “mid or late February” timing is slightly off, but he is clearly referring to the then-upcoming deadline for the recall drive.
* **Signatures collected by mid–late February 2021:** By **February 17, 2021**, recall organizers publicly claimed to have collected about **1.7 million total signatures**, already exceeding the 1.5 million target in raw count (before official validation). ([wsws.org](https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2021/02/22/cali-f22.html?utm_source=openai))  Around the same period, California officials reported about 1.1 million submitted signatures, with hundreds of thousands still to be processed, indicating the campaign was on track to meet or exceed the required number. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2021/02/20/newsom-recall-million-signatures?utm_source=openai))
* **Official validation and triggering of recall:** The Secretary of State later reported that by the March 2021 deadline, **2,117,730** signatures had been submitted, with **1,719,943** ultimately deemed valid—well above the 1,495,709 requirement. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_California_gubernatorial_recall_election?utm_source=openai))  On **April 26, 2021**, the Secretary of State formally announced that the threshold of verified signatures had been met, thereby triggering the next phase of the recall process. ([sos.ca.gov](https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2021-news-releases-and-advisories/sw21019?utm_source=openai))  This led to the certified 2021 California gubernatorial recall election against Newsom.

Because the organizers did indeed secure more than the required number of signatures in time to trigger a recall election, Chamath’s substantive prediction—that *“they’re going to get the votes”* and force a recall—was **right**, even though he was slightly imprecise about the exact calendar deadline.

predictions.grok_explanation: Chamath predicted organizers would obtain the required signatures by a deadline in 'mid- or late-February 2021.' However, the actual circulation deadline was March 17, 2021, extended from November 17, 2020, by court order due to COVID-19 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_California_gubernatorial_recall_election); [SOS PDF](https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/newsom-heatlie-fourth.pdf)). Required signatures: 1,495,709. By late February (e.g., Feb 19: 1.09M submitted, claimed 1.7M total per [Deadline](https://deadline.com/2021/02/gavin-newsom-recall-million-signatures-1234697678/); Feb 21: >1M per [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2021/02/21/politics/newsom-california-recall-signatures)), they had not reached the threshold. Full submission: 2.1M by March 17; verified sufficient April 26, 2021. Thus, they did not meet it by late February, making the timing-specific prediction wrong, though a recall election occurred later.

predictions.explanation:
The next episode after E16 is E17, **“Big Tech bans Trump, ramifications for the First Amendment & the open Internet,”** released on January 11, 2021, three days after E16 on January 8, 2021.([allinpodcastsummary.com](https://allinpodcastsummary.com/?utm_source=openai))  

Between those dates, at least one event clearly fits *“highly unexpected and highly impactful”*:

- On January 8, 2021, Twitter **permanently suspended Donald Trump’s @realDonaldTrump account**, an unprecedented move against a sitting (then-outgoing) U.S. president and a major shift in platform governance. Multiple outlets documented this as a permanent ban due to the risk of further incitement of violence.([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/jan/08/donald-trump-twitter-ban-suspended?utm_source=openai))  
- In the same window, Amazon Web Services cut off hosting for Parler, and the site went offline on January 11, 2021, after Apple and Google had already removed its app—another major, widely covered escalation in Big Tech’s moderation response to the Capitol riot.([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2021/01/11/parler-is-officially-offline-after-aws-suspension/?utm_source=openai))  

E17 itself is devoted to discussing these bans, which the hosts treat as a major, consequential development.([allinpodcastsummary.com](https://allinpodcastsummary.com/?utm_source=openai))  Given that at least one such event (Trump’s permanent Twitter ban, plus the coordinated deplatforming of Parler) occurred between E16 and the next recording/release, Friedberg’s prediction that **“some highly unexpected and highly impactful thing will occur” before they next met** was borne out.
